overview.text: The Troubles were decades of political and sectarian conflict centered on Northern Ireland from the late 1960s into the 1990s. The conflict concerned Northern Ireland's place in the United Kingdom, competing national identities, civil rights, and the use of violence by armed groups. Unionists generally favored remaining in the United Kingdom, while nationalists sought closer ties or unity with Ireland. The 1998 Belfast, or Good Friday, Agreement created a power-sharing framework and recognized that any change in Northern Ireland's constitutional status required majority consent. It also addressed rights, security, policing, and prisoners. The agreement was a major peace settlement, though reconciliation remained an ongoing process.

key_facts.text: The Troubles lasted about three decades before the 1998 agreement.
The Belfast Agreement was signed on 10 April 1998.
The agreement established power-sharing through an Assembly and Executive.
Northern Ireland's constitutional status cannot change without majority consent.
The agreement recognized the right to identify as British, Irish, or both.

overview.text: The Meiji Restoration was the transfer of political authority from Japan's Tokugawa shogunate to a government acting in the name of Emperor Meiji. The shogun gave up authority in 1867, and a new imperial government took shape in 1868 amid domestic strains and pressure from Western powers. Its leaders introduced sweeping political, social, and economic reforms, while studying foreign technology and institutions. The Charter Oath of 1868 called for deliberation in public affairs, and a central administrative system gradually replaced older arrangements. The changes helped turn Japan into a more centralized and industrializing state, but the word 'restoration' should not suggest a simple return to an earlier system.

key_facts.text: The last Tokugawa shogun resigned his authority in 1867.
A new imperial government was established in 1868.
The Charter Oath was promulgated in 1868.
The Meiji government invited foreign advisers and sent missions abroad.
The new government's Grand Council of State system took shape in the early 1870s.

overview.text: The Tang dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907 CE, following the short-lived Sui dynasty. Its government drew on Sui institutions while expanding trade, diplomacy, and military influence. Chang'an, the capital, attracted merchants, religious travelers, and envoys from many parts of Asia and beyond. The examination system gave some educated men a route into government service outside old aristocratic networks. Tang cultural life is especially remembered for poetry: Li Bai, also called Li Bo, and Du Fu are major figures. The An Lushan rebellion in the eighth century weakened the court, but Tang rule continued for many more generations. Its art and literature remained models for later generations.

key_facts.text: The Tang dynasty lasted from 618 to 907 CE.
The Sui dynasty preceded the Tang and helped establish institutions it used.
Chang'an was a cosmopolitan Tang capital.
Imperial examinations widened access to government office for educated men.
Li Bai and Du Fu were celebrated Tang poets.
The An Lushan rebellion weakened the dynasty in the eighth century.

overview.text: The Yuan dynasty was the Mongol-ruled dynasty of China, conventionally dated 1271 to 1368. Kublai Khan founded it as Mongol rulers took the title and institutions of Chinese emperors. Its capital was Dadu, also called Khanbaliq, on the site of present-day Beijing. Yuan rule connected China to the much wider Mongol world while also adapting Chinese administrative and cultural practices. Artists continued to develop painting and calligraphy under the dynasty. By the mid-fourteenth century, court factionalism, corruption, disasters, and rebellion weakened its rule. In 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang displaced the Yuan in China and established the Ming dynasty, beginning a new imperial era.

key_facts.text: The Yuan dynasty is commonly dated 1271–1368.
Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty.
The Mongol capital Dadu was also called Khanbaliq and is now Beijing.
Yuan rulers adopted Chinese political and cultural models.
Zhu Yuanzhang established the Ming dynasty in 1368 after ousting the Yuan in China.

overview.text: A tank is an armored combat vehicle designed to move across difficult ground while carrying weapons and protecting its crew. Continuous tracks helped early tanks cross obstacles, while armor shielded crews from small-arms fire. Britain developed the first combat tanks during the trench warfare of World War I, hoping to cross trenches, wire, and machine-gun positions. The British Mark I entered battle on the Somme on 15 September 1916. Early machines were slow and often broke down, so their arrival did not by itself end the stalemate. Tanks later became a major part of combined-arms warfare, used alongside infantry and other forces.

key_facts.text: The British Mark I was the first tank to see combat.
Mark I tanks first fought on 15 September 1916 at the Somme.
Male Mark I tanks carried six-pounder guns; female versions mounted machine guns.
Early tanks were designed to cross trenches and confront machine-gun positions.
Mechanical problems prevented many Mark I tanks from reaching their start points.

overview.text: Osama bin Laden was a leader of the militant organization al-Qaeda. During the war against Soviet forces in Afghanistan, he raised money and gained connections among foreign volunteers. In 1988 he and other leaders formed al-Qaeda, which later organized terrorist operations across national borders. The 9/11 Commission describes bin Laden as head of the organization; al-Qaeda carried out the September 11, 2001 attacks in the United States. After years of pursuit, U.S. forces killed him during an operation in Abbottabad, Pakistan, in May 2011. His death removed the group's longtime leader but did not mean the organization or its affiliates immediately disappeared.

key_facts.text: Bin Laden and a small group of leaders created al-Qaeda in 1988.
He raised money for foreign volunteers during the Afghanistan war against Soviet forces.
Al-Qaeda carried out the September 11, 2001 attacks.
Bin Laden led al-Qaeda for more than two decades.
U.S. forces killed him in Abbottabad, Pakistan, in May 2011.

overview.text: Selim I ruled the Ottoman Empire from 1512 to 1520 and greatly expanded its territory. In 1514 his army defeated the Safavid forces of Shah Ismail I at the Battle of Chaldiran, a major Ottoman victory on the empire's eastern frontier. Selim then campaigned against the Mamluk Sultanate. Ottoman armies conquered Syria and Egypt in 1516–1517, ending Mamluk rule there and bringing these lands into the Ottoman realm. The expansion also placed the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina under Ottoman authority. Selim's relatively short reign therefore reshaped the balance of power across the Middle East and set the stage for the empire inherited by his successor.

key_facts.text: Selim I reigned from 1512 to 1520.
He defeated Shah Ismail I's Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514.
Ottoman armies conquered Syria and Egypt in 1516–1517.
These conquests ended the Mamluk sultanate.
Mecca and Medina came under Ottoman authority during Selim's rule.

overview.text: Muammar Gaddafi took power in Libya in 1969 and dominated the country's politics for more than four decades. His government used the language of popular rule, which he developed in The Green Book, but a Library of Congress country profile described the system as authoritarian and centered on Gaddafi and his close circle. In 2011 an uprising challenged his rule, and his government tried to suppress it. Opposition forces captured him near Sirte in October 2011, and he died that day. The exact circumstances of his death remain disputed; Human Rights Watch reported that available forensic evidence could not establish the cause with certainty. His fall ended a long dictatorship.

key_facts.text: Gaddafi became Libya's de facto leader in September 1969.
The Green Book presented his political ideas and 'Jamahiriya' system.
Despite claims of popular rule, Gaddafi exercised real authority through an authoritarian system.
An uprising against his regime began in 2011.
Gaddafi died after capture near Sirte on 20 October 2011.
Human Rights Watch found the precise cause of death uncertain.

overview.text: The Iroquois Confederacy is also called the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, using the peoples' own name. It began as an alliance of five nations: Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca. The Tuscarora later joined, giving rise to the name Six Nations. Each nation kept its own identity while participating in a shared political system shaped by the Great Law of Peace. A Grand Council makes decisions by consensus, and clan mothers have important roles in community and leadership. The confederacy's origins are preserved in Haudenosaunee accounts of the Peacemaker and the Great Law. Haudenosaunee nations and their government continue today.

The Tuscarora became the sixth nation in 1722, according to Smithsonian educational material.

overview.text: Guatemala is a Central American country whose modern history includes a U.S.-backed overthrow and a long internal armed conflict. President Jacobo Árbenz pursued land reform in the early 1950s. The U.S. Central Intelligence Agency supported a plan to remove him; after invasion, propaganda, and pressure on the army in June 1954, Árbenz resigned. Later conflict between the government and the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unity lasted for decades. A 1996 peace agreement formally ended the war and set out commitments concerning human rights, displaced people, and Indigenous peoples. These events show how land, political power, and foreign intervention shaped Guatemala's twentieth century.

The CIA backed a plan to overthrow Árbenz.
Árbenz resigned on 27 June 1954 after invasion and pressure.
The 1996 agreement was between Guatemala's government and the URNG.
The peace agreement recognized rights of displaced people and Indigenous peoples.
